name: Prize crossword No 26,699
preamble: Solutions to four across and four down clues require a letter to be changed before entry in the grid. All these eight entries are of a kind.

clue.text: Racy? Live, live, live, flower!

blocks.note: blue as in risqué or smutty, like a blue joke
to live is to be, to exist
L marks the live wire on an electrical plug
the same wiring abbreviation used a second time

explanation.surface: An excitable cry urging a wild life, ending with a cheer for a flower.
explanation.walkthrough: The three repeats of 'live' look like one chant, but each is read separately: once as the verb BE, then twice as L, the label for the live terminal on a plug.
explanation.definitionFit: The bluebell is a woodland plant with nodding blue bell-shaped blooms, common in British springtime.

clue.text: Senate and people of Rome question being replaced by head of union branch

indicators.note: when one thing is replaced by another, a single letter is swapped out for a new one
the head is the top or front, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: SPQR abbreviates the Latin Senatus Populusque Romanus
Q is the standard abbreviation for question; this letter is removed
the first letter of union

explanation.surface: A history lesson in which Rome's famous motto gets rewritten by a trade union branch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head of' picks the opening letter of 'union', which takes the place of the Q in the Roman abbreviation. 'Branch' looks like part of the union phrase but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A spur is a side line branching off a main railway, road or ridge.

clue.text: Still without its first back bar retailer

indicators.note: going without the opening letter means that initial is dropped
going back means running the other way, so these letters are read right to left

blocks.note: even, as in 'even now' or 'still more'
a rod is a bar of metal or wood

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper who is still behind the bar, minus something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' means 'even' here, as in 'still better'; losing its E leaves VEN, and the bar turned round supplies the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A vendor is someone who sells goods, and a retailer sells them to the public.

clue.text: Put down a biblical teacher

blocks.note: taken as written
the scribes were teachers of the Jewish law in the Gospels

explanation.surface: Someone humiliates a religious instructor from scripture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put down' suggests insulting someone, but here it means attributing, as in 'put it down to tiredness'.
explanation.definitionFit: To ascribe a result to a cause is to attribute it, the same idiom as putting it down to that cause.

clue.text: Blue left in stick

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: gum is glue, which sticks things together
L is the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A sad person stranded in a sticky spot.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue builds GLUM, meaning blue in the sense of sad; per the preamble its G is then changed to P to make the fruit PLUM, one of eight themed entries.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling blue means feeling low and miserable, which is exactly what glum describes.

clue.text: Just a bit firm, oysters from here

blocks.note: a whit is the smallest amount, as in 'not a whit'
stable means steady and firm

explanation.surface: A cook testing whether oysters are slightly firm, and asking where they came from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just a bit firm' reads like a description of the shellfish, but it is two pieces of wordplay. Whitstable is a seaside town in Kent, England.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kent town of Whitstable has been famous for its native oyster beds since Roman times.

clue.text: Rig out the second person who was keen?

definitions.note: the verb: to wail in lament

indicators.note: something put out of order is disarranged, so these letters get rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
in Genesis Eve was the second human, after Adam

explanation.surface: Dressing up the second-placed person, who was apparently enthusiastic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keen' looks like the adjective for eager, but it is the verb meaning to wail for the dead; 'second person' is not grammatical 'you' but Eve.
explanation.definitionFit: To keen is to lament loudly over a death, an Irish-rooted word for mourning aloud in sorrow.

clue.text: Thatch reducers' craft?

blocks.note: first meaning: tools for cutting hair, thatch being slang for a head of hair
second meaning: fast sailing ships of the nineteenth century

explanation.surface: Asking about the trade of the people who trim straw roofs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thatch' suggests a roof, but it is jokey slang for hair; 'craft' looks like skill or trade but means boats.
explanation.definitionFit: Hair trimmers are called clippers, and the tall, swift merchant sailing ships of the tea trade were also clippers.

clue.text: Operetta composer: "Pardon one's falling between two extremes"

indicators.note: whatever falls between lands in the gap, so it ends up enclosed by the outer letters

blocks.note: left and right are the two extremes of a political or physical spectrum
'eh?' is what you say when you didn't catch something
a means one

explanation.surface: A quotation in which an operetta composer asks forgiveness for someone falling.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is short for 'is'. Franz Lehár was the Hungarian composer of The Merry Widow.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Lehár wrote light stage works such as The Merry Widow, the operetta genre at its most popular.

clue.text: Fly's salty secretion

blocks.note: first meaning: to rush along at speed
second meaning: a drop of liquid from the eye

explanation.walkthrough: Both meanings point to TEAR; per the preamble one letter then changes, T becoming P, to give the fruit PEAR, one of eight themed entries.
explanation.definitionFit: To tear is to dash along quickly, and a tear is the briny drop shed when crying.

clue.text: Day before vessel problem is an elusive major universal influence

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for day
Noah's ark was a vessel
as in 'what's the matter?'

explanation.surface: A sailor's worry, the day before a voyage, about some vague force.
explanation.walkthrough: 'before' simply puts the day first. 'Universal' here means of the universe, not general.
explanation.definitionFit: Physicists infer this invisible substance from its gravity; it is never seen directly yet shapes galaxies across the cosmos.

clue.text: Street trader cyclist casually reported

indicators.note: something reported is spoken, and said casually the syllables run together

blocks.note: a cyclist pedals, so is a pedaller

explanation.surface: A hawker on the street was, people loosely said, a bike rider.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue gives PEDLAR; per the preamble its P becomes M, giving the fruit MEDLAR, one of eight themed entries.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedlar travels about selling small goods, a classic street trader or hawker.

clue.text: Adriana, lip-curling Stones connoisseur

definitions.note: the word is more often an adjective; here used as a noun

indicators.note: curling bends and twists things out of their shape, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman sneering in the manner of a Rolling Stones fan.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital S makes 'Stones' look like the rock band, but it means gemstones; 'lip-curling' paints a Jagger sneer.
explanation.definitionFit: Lapidary work is the cutting and engraving of gems, so a lapidarian is an expert in precious stones.

clue.text: Having something on top, getting at the bananas in the sack

indicators.note: going bananas is going crazy, so these letters run wild
to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: the sack is slang for bed, as in 'hit the sack'
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone has a pile on their head after raiding the bananas in a bag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the sack' is bed; 'bananas' looks like fruit in the sack but signals the scramble.
explanation.definitionFit: Behatted means wearing a hat, and a hat is something worn on top of the head.

clue.text: Poetic invocation used in local round dance

indicators.note: turning something round faces it the opposite way, so its letters run backwards
something used in another is placed inside it

blocks.note: a local is a pub, and PH is the map abbreviation for public house
'O' opens poetic addresses such as 'O Captain!'

explanation.surface: A line of verse calling out during a traditional circle dance at the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round dance' looks like one phrase but 'round' reverses the pub. The clue gives HOP; per the preamble O becomes I, giving the fruit HIP, as in rose hip.
explanation.definitionFit: A hop is an informal dance party, as in a sock hop or village hop.

clue.text: Down to bra and panties, exit discreetly?

definitions.note: a state reached rather than the action; the phrasal verb is what gets you there

blocks.note: first meaning: to shed an outer garment, leaving only underwear
second meaning: to leave quietly without fuss

explanation.surface: Someone has stripped to their underwear and wonders about sneaking out.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half describes the result of removing a dress; the second is the idiom for leaving unnoticed.
explanation.definitionFit: You slip off a dress to remove it easily, and you slip off from a party when sneaking away unnoticed.

clue.text: Raising of flag, ultimately obscure

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising lifts the letters upward, so they read bottom to top
ultimately points to the very end, so only the closing letter is used

blocks.note: taken as written, then turned upside down
the final letter of flag

explanation.surface: Hoisting a flag, in the end, does nothing but hide things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raising of flag' reads as one phrase, but 'of' is the word being raised. The clue gives FOG; per the preamble O becomes I, giving the fruit FIG.
explanation.definitionFit: To fog something is to cloud it so it cannot be seen clearly, which is to make it unclear.

clue.text: People are jetted by this airline in singular way

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular
a path is a way
BA is British Airways

explanation.surface: Passengers are flown somewhere by this one carrier in its own distinctive style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jetted' and 'airline' suggest flying, but the jets are water jets in a tub.
explanation.definitionFit: A spa bath has underwater nozzles that send pressurised streams over the bather, so people in it really are jetted.

clue.text: Having a fling, working at the wheel?

blocks.note: first meaning: tossing or hurling something
second meaning: shaping clay pots on a potter's wheel

explanation.surface: Someone enjoys a brief affair while driving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fling' suggests a romance and 'the wheel' suggests driving; both are misdirection, one for hurling and one for pottery.
explanation.definitionFit: A fling is a hurl, and potters describe forming clay on a revolving wheel as throwing a pot.

clue.text: Make water boil for Earl Grey etc

blocks.note: making water is a polite phrase for urinating
to boil with anger is to rage

explanation.surface: Instructions for brewing a cup of the bergamot-scented tea.
explanation.walkthrough: Earl Grey is a tea, but here it is read as a nobleman: Earl Grey was a British prime minister and a peer.
explanation.definitionFit: The peerage is the whole body of titled nobles, such as earls, dukes and barons, of whom an earl is one.

clue.text: Railway's Capital Rover, say, terminated outside French region

indicators.note: a capital is the top or head, so only the opening letter is taken
one piece sits outside, wrapping around another

blocks.note: something done is finished
the first letter of railway
Rover is a typical name for a dog

explanation.surface: A train company's London-area travel pass, now discontinued, abroad in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital Rover' looks like a London rail ticket, but 'Capital' attaches to Railway; 'say' marks Rover as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dordogne is a department of south-west France, named after its river and popular with British visitors.

clue.text: Superior's performing drunk

blocks.note: a performer is on stage
high means intoxicated

explanation.surface: The boss is putting on a show while intoxicated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Superior' looks like a noun for a boss, but it is the adjective for being above, and the 's is 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something on high is placed above, in a loftier position, which is what superior literally means.

clue.text: Jolly blubber-covered male hogging centre of bed

indicators.note: the centre is the middle, so only the middle letter is used
something covered has another wrapped around it
to hog is to keep to oneself, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: to blubber is to cry
he is the male pronoun
the middle letter of bed

explanation.surface: A cheerful fat man taking up the middle of the bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blubber' looks like fat, fitting the jolly man, but it is the verb to weep. The clue gives CHEERY; per the preamble an E becomes R, giving the fruit CHERRY.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheery means bright and good-humoured, a close synonym of jolly.

clue.text: Baby salad ingredient collection

blocks.note: cos is a variety of lettuce, romaine in the US
a set is a collection

explanation.surface: A selection of tiny salad leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Baby' looks like an adjective, as in baby leaves, but it is the verb meaning to pamper.
explanation.definitionFit: To baby someone is to treat them with excessive care and indulgence, which is to cosset or pamper them.

clue.text: Rebuke: for instance, "shrill tart"

blocks.note: first meaning: a harsh telling-off
second meaning: both quoted terms are adjectives that mean keen or acute

explanation.surface: A rude jibe calling a woman a shrill tart.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted phrase looks like an insult, but each of its terms is a synonym of sharp: a shrill sound and a tart taste.
explanation.definitionFit: A rebuke is a reprimand delivered in cutting language; and shrill and tart are literally vocabulary meaning acute or acidic.

clue.text: Question about English dairy product

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: why is a question word
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Someone queries a particular English cheese or milk item.
explanation.walkthrough: The question word wraps round the abbreviation for English.
explanation.definitionFit: Whey is the watery liquid left after milk curdles in cheesemaking, a by-product of the dairy.

clue.text: Green hanky material?

blocks.note: first meaning: a stretch of mown grass
second meaning: a fine linen or cotton fabric

explanation.walkthrough: 'Green' looks like a colour describing the hanky, but it is a noun, a grassy area.
explanation.definitionFit: A green is a patch of mown grass, and lawn is also a sheer fine cloth traditionally used for handkerchiefs.

clue.text: Halt (as they used to say) – that's no way to serve up a lettuce!

definitions.text: that's no way to serve up a lettuce

blocks.note: first meaning: in old usage, to walk lamely

blocks.clueFragment: that's no way to serve up a lettuce
blocks.note: second meaning: wilted and floppy, as stale salad leaves are

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned cry to stop a waiter bringing out a sad salad.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue gives LIMP; per the preamble P becomes E, giving the fruit LIME. 'Halt' looks like 'stop' but is the archaic verb, which the bracket flags.
explanation.definitionFit: In older English to halt meant to walk unevenly through lameness, and a wilted salad leaf is floppy rather than crisp.

clue.text: Super-sounding grid

indicators.note: sounding means as heard by the ear, not as spelt

blocks.note: super means great, which is said just like the fireplace grid

explanation.walkthrough: The clue gives GRATE; per the preamble its T becomes P, giving the fruit GRAPE, one of eight themed entries.
explanation.definitionFit: A grate is a metal grid or framework of bars, such as the one holding fuel in a fireplace.

clue.text: Grand Midlands town not about to go flashy

indicators.note: turned about means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards
something that is to go is to be removed

blocks.note: G is short for grand, a thousand pounds
Leamington Spa is a town in Warwickshire, in the English Midlands
taken as written; turned round it is removed from the town

explanation.surface: A great town in the English Midlands refuses to become showy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not about' reverses to TON, which goes from the end of the town's name. 'Grand' looks like an adjective for the town but is G.
explanation.definitionFit: Gleaming means shining brightly, and something flashy is showy and bright to the eye.
